{{short description|Partial order in lattice theory}}

In [[order theory]], the '''strong set order''' <math>\leq_s</math> is a [[partial order]] over the subsets of a [[lattice]]. It is widely used to study [[monotone comparative statics]] of [[Parametric programming|parametrized optimization problems]] in [[economic theory]] and [[operations research]].<ref name = "topkis1998">{{cite book |last1=Topkis |first1=Donald M. |title=Supermodularity and Complementarity |date=1998 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=9780691032443 |page=32}}</ref>

The strong set order was first defined and used by [[Arthur F. Veinott]] in his unpublished lecture notes.<ref name="topkis1978">{{cite journal |last1=Topkis |first1=Donald M. |title=Minimizing a Submodular Function on a Lattice |journal=Operations Research |date=1978 |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=305–321 |doi=10.1287/opre.26.2.305 |jstor=169636 |quote=Veinott (personal communication) introduced this relation.}}</ref><ref name = "milgrom1994">{{cite journal |last1=Milgrom |first1=Paul |last2=Chris |first2=Shannon |author1-link=Paul Milgrom |title=Monotone Comparative Statics |journal=Econometrica |date=1994 |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=157–180 |doi=10.2307/2951479 |jstor=2951479 |quote=(...) the strong set order <math>\leq_s</math>, introduced by Veinott (1989).}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Veinott |first1=Arthur F. |title=Lattice Programming |journal=Unpublished Notes from Lectures Delivered at Johns Hopkins University |date=1989}}</ref> It was later popularized by [[Donald M. Topkis]], [[Paul Milgrom]] and [[Chris Shannon]] via their work on [[monotone comparative statics]], in particular through [[Topkis's Theorem| Topkis' Theorem]].

== Definition ==

Given a [[Lattice (order)| lattice]] <math>(X, \leq)</math>, consider its [[power set]] <math>\mathcal P(X)</math>. The '''strong set order''' <math>\leq_s</math> is a [[partial order]] on <math>\mathcal P(X)</math> given by:

:<math>
A \leq_s B \iff \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
  a \vee b \in B \\[0.1em]
  a \wedge b \in A
\end{array} 
\ \ \ \ \ \forall a \in A, b \in B,
\right.
</math>

where <math>a \vee b</math> and <math>a \wedge b</math> are respectively the [[join and meet]] of <math>a, b</math>.

== Examples and non-examples ==

=== Real numbers ===

Consider the real numbers <math>\mathbb R</math> with the usual order <math>\geq</math>. Let <math>A = [\underline a, \overline a]</math> and <math>B = [\underline b, \overline b]</math>. Then 

:<math>A \leq_s  B \iff \underline a \leq \underline b \ \text{ and } \ \overline a \leq \overline b</math>.

More generally, for any <math>A, B \subseteq \mathbb R</math>, we have

:<math>A \leq_s  B \iff \inf A \leq \inf B \ \text{ and } \ \sup A \leq \sup B</math>.

=== Euclidean space ===

Consider the [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb R^n</math> with the usual pointwise order: <math>\mathbf x \leq \mathbf y \iff x_i \leq y_i \ \ \forall i \leq n</math>. For <math>n = 2</math>, let

:<math>A = [0,2] \times [0, 3],</math>

:<math>B = [1,3] \times [1, 4].</math>

Then :<math> A \leq_s B</math>. But now consider

:<math>B' = [-1, 3] \times [1,4]</math>;

Then <math>A \nleq_s B'</math>, since <math>(0, 0) \in A </math>, <math> (-1, 1) \in B'</math> but

:<math>(0, 0) \wedge (-1, 1) = (-1, 0) \notin B' </math>.

=== Power set ===

Consider the [[power set]] of the [[natural numbers]] <math>\mathcal P(\mathbb N)</math> under the [[Inclusion order|set-inclusion order]]: <math>A \leq B \iff A \subseteq B</math>. Let

:<math>A = \{\{1\}\}</math>,

:<math>B = \{\{1\}, \{2\}, \{1,2,3\}\}</math>.

It it ''not true'' that <math>A \leq_s B</math>. Indeed, we have <math>\{1\} \in A</math>, <math>\{2\} \in B</math>, but

:<math>\{1\} \wedge \{2\} = \{1\} \cap \{2\} = \varnothing \notin A,</math>

whence <math>A \nleq_s B</math>.

== Applications ==

=== Topkis' Theorem ===

The strong set order is widely used in [[monotone comparative statics]], in particular via [[Topkis's Theorem| Topkis' Theorem]]. Given a lattice <math>X</math>, a [[poset]] <math>\Theta</math>, a [[constrained optimization|constraint]] [[Set-valued function| correspondence]] <math>D : \Theta \rightrightarrows X</math> and a function <math>f : X \times \Theta \to \mathbb R</math>, the theorem gives sufficient conditions for the correspondence 

<math>x^*(\theta) = \arg\max_{x \in D(\theta)} f(x, \theta)</math>

the be increasing in the strong set order, that is, for the statement

:<math>\theta \geq \theta' \implies x^*(\theta) \geq_s x^*(\theta')</math>

to hold.

=== Monotone selections === 

Increasigness in the strong set order can be used to obtain monotone [[Choice function|selection]]s from [[Set-valued function| correspondence]]s. Indeed, if <math>X </math> is a [[poset]] and <math> Y</math> is a lattice, the correspondence  <math>\Gamma : X \rightrightarrows Y</math> is nonempty-valued and increasing in the strong set order, then a monotone selection <math>g</math> from <math>\Gamma</math> exists if any of the following hold:

* <math>\Gamma(x) \subseteq Y</math> has a minimal element for every <math>x \in X</math> (in particular, if <math>\Gamma</math> is [[Complete lattice|complete-lattice]]-valued). One can thus take :<math>g : X \to Y</math> by putting <math>g(x) = \min \Gamma(x)</math>. The same works if a maximal element is available. 

* <math>Y</math> is a [[lattice (order)#Sublattices| sublattice]] of a finite [[cartesian product|product]] of [[Total_order#Chains| chain]]s.<ref name="kukushkin2013">{{cite journal |last1=Kukushikin |first1=Nikolai S. |title=Increasing Selections from Increasing Multifunctions |journal=Order |date=2013 |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=541–555 |doi=10.1007/s11083-012-9260-6 }}</ref> This covers, for example, <math>Y \subseteq \mathbb R^n</math>.

* <math>X</math> is countable.<ref name="kukushkin2013"></ref>

=== Zhou's Fixed-Point Theorem for correspondences ===

The strong set order can also be used for a generalization of [[Knaster–Tarski theorem| Tarski's fixed-point theorem]] to [[set-valued function|correspondences]] known as Zhou's fixed-point theorem:<ref name="zhou1994">{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Zhou |title=The Set of Nash Equilibria of a Supermodular Game Is a Complete Lattice |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |date=1994 |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=295–300 |doi=10.1006/game.1994.1051 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Lu |title=Fixed point theorems for increasing correspondences on lattices |journal=Economic Theory |date=2026 |volume=68 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1007/s00199-026-01702-7 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

'''Theorem:''' let <math>X</math> be a nonempty [[complete lattice]] and <math>\Gamma : X \rightrightarrows X</math> a nonempty-valued correspondence. If <math>\Gamma</math> is increasing in the strong set order and <math>\Gamma(x)</math> is a [[Complete lattice#Complete sublattices|subcomplete sublattice]] for all <math>x \in X</math>, then <math>\Gamma</math> has a fixed point. Moreover, the set <math>\text{Fix}(\Gamma)</math> of such fixed points is a complete lattice.

== Weak set order ==

The strong set order if often too restrictive for some applications, in particular because it assumes that the underlying space <math>X</math> is a lattice.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1= Che|first1=Yeon-Koo |author-link1= Yeon-Koo Che|last2= Kim|first2=Jinwoo |author-link2= | last3 = Kojima |first3 = Fuhito |author-link3 = Fuhito Kojima |date=2021 |title=Weak Monotone Comparative Statics |pages=2–3|eprint=1911.06442v4 |class= econ.TH|quote= |mode= }}</ref> A useful weaker ordering which can be used on the subsets of any [[poset]] <math>X</math> is the weak set order <math>\leq_w</math>, defined by:<ref name = "topkis1998"></ref>

:<math>
A \leq_w B \iff \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
  \forall a \in A \ \ \exists b \in B \ \text{ such that } a \leq b, \text{ and } \\[0.1em]
  \forall b \in B \ \ \exists a \in A \ \text{ such that } b \geq a.
\end{array} 
\right.
</math>

This order can moreover be broken down into two weaker orders: the upper and lower weak set orders <math>\leq_{uw}, \leq_{lw}</math>, respectively defined by:

:<math>
A \leq_{uw} B \iff \forall a \in A \ \ \exists b \in B \ \text{ such that } a \leq b,
</math>

:<math>
A \leq_{lw} B \iff \forall b \in B \ \ \exists a \in A \ \text{ such that } b \leq a.
</math>

Clearly <math>A \leq_w B \iff A \leq_{uw} B \text{ and } A \leq_{lw} B</math>.
